When designing a government tool or service, you should always start by learning about the people who will use it. If you don’t understand users or what they need from your service, you cannot build the right thing.

You should involve diverse stakeholders in the design and testing process and undertake thorough user research and public engagement to ensure you’re including the views of those that may be affected or digitally excluded.

You must understand and comply with your legal obligations and duties. Refer to the Public Sector Equality Duty (PSED) and the Equality Act 2010.
Describe the measures you will take to protect research particpants.

You must take steps to protect research participants. This applies to your team and to any third-party researchers you work with. 

You should:
o make sure that participants understand the research and any risks involved 
o only include participants who give clear, informed consent without pressure or coercion 
o allow participants to withdraw at any time (with exceptions for situations like medical research where participant information is anonymised and aggregated and cannot be removed from the research data set)
o anonymise all data used in reports or analysis.

The Service Manual has guidance on [managing user research data and participant privacy].
Describe the measures you will take to protect researchers.

Some research projects involve sensitive topics, such as child protection or adult safeguarding. These can be distressing for both researchers and participants. To reduce risk, you should:
o highlight any sensitive topics in workshop or interview plans
o set up a ‘safety check-in’ protocol to support staff after sessions, particularly for one-to-one or lone working
o use existing ethical guidelines and processes, such as the Service Manual’s guidance on researching emotionally sensitive subjects

In rare cases, researchers may be targeted by participants or others. If this happens, or if the risk is known in advance, put safeguards in place to protect staff.

The Government Analysis Function provides a list of resources related to conducting research and analysis in government.

Briefly explain the environmental and sustainability implications of your project.

Environmental sustainability means thinking about the wider impact of your project on people and the planet. It’s important to consider this from the start, as it can influence your choices about tools, suppliers and infrastructure.

The environmental sustainability chapter in the Data and AI Ethics Framework provides further advice on how to assess the potential impact of data and AI projects.
Briefly describe how you intend to monitor, evaluate and address environmental impact and sustainability challenges.

Before you begin building a tool or system, you should develop a plan to monitor and evaluate the environmental impact.

You should think about factors such as: 
o Whether AI is the best technology or tool for the task – there may be alternatives that provide as good, or better, results and require less resource-intensive training and development.
o Project size and complexity – how much data will be processed, the number of end users, bandwidth and latency requirements, prompt efficiency
o Software requirements – including model type.
o Hardware requirements – such as data centre usage or Internet of Things (IoT) devices.

The Service Manual also has guidance on how to build more [environmentally sustainable digital services in government].
